title: CI fixers and the false-heal check

story: Tuesday, 10:09. The gather window is over and the CI fixer has its VM. It runs the failing test from main and sees it fail for itself: a refactor merged at 10:02 changed one comparison, and now the empty projects table no longer shows its "No projects yet" card. The test that checks the card is red, exactly as it should be.

The fixer's job is to make CI green, and there are two ways to do that. It can fix the comparison in the component, one line. Or it can change the test: skip it, delete the assertion, or edit the expected text to match what the broken code now returns. Every one of those turns CI green. Only the first one fixes main. The others hide the bug, and the next person to look at a green main has no idea the card is gone.
hook.question: How do we make sure a fixer can never turn CI green by weakening the test that caught the problem?

p: Before any fix, the CI fixer answers one question: is the failure in our code at all? It runs the failed job's commands at main's newest commit, inside its VM. If they pass there, the code is fine and the problem is the environment, a runner, the package mirror, the QA environment, or a flaky test. The fixer posts its evidence to #ai-agents-alerts and stops, because no code change can fix an environment. If the commands fail in the VM too, the failure is real and reproducible, and the fixer makes the smallest change it can inside its charter's paths.

Each fixer keeps a small map of how to reproduce every CI job in its VM, and which jobs it must always hand to a person. This lesson is about what happens after the fixer is sure the code is broken, because that is where the dangerous shortcut lives.

code.text:
workflow: "[FRONTEND] - CI"
setup: cd frontend && npm ci
check_main_first: true          # failed commands green at main's head: environment or flake
jobs:
  "Unit Tests":
    vm: lite
    repro:
      - cd frontend && npm run check-types
      - cd frontend && npm run lint
      - cd frontend && npm run test:unit
  "I&T - AWS":
    vm: full
    repro: ["cd frontend && npx playwright test --project=pr <failed spec>"]   # against FCP Lab
    if_green_in_lab: hand_off   # failed on QA, passes on the Lab: the QA environment, not code
  "Deploy": { hand_off: "needs cloud credentials; DevOps" }

notes.text: Run the failed commands at main's head first. Green there means it is not our code.
The job's exact name in frontend CI, and the commands that reproduce it.
An integration test that fails against the QA environment but passes against FCP Lab, the full product on one machine with fake data, is a hand-off.
The VM holds no cloud credentials, so deploy failures always go to a person.

read.h: Two ways to turn CI green
p: A false heal is a change that turns CI green by weakening the checks instead of fixing the code. It comes in a few shapes, and all of them are easy for an agent that has been told to make CI pass: delete a test file, skip a test with it.skip or @pytest.mark.skip, remove an assertion, change an expected value to match the broken output, or loosen a threshold such as a coverage minimum, a retry count or a timeout. A model does not need bad intent to do this. It needs only a goal, "make CI green", and a moment where the shortcut looks reasonable.

We do not ask the model to promise it will not do this, and we do not rely on a reviewer to spot it in a long diff. A false heal leaves marks in the diff that a short program can find every time: a removed line with an assertion, an added line with .skip(, a number after retries that went up. So the false-heal check is plain code that reads the diff. It is cheap, it never gets tired, and an agent cannot talk it out of its answer.

The check gets the diff as a list of files, each with its added and removed lines, and the charter's never-list. Every rule is one regular expression and one comparison. Two of them deserve a closer look. Counting assertions catches a removed assertion, but not a changed one: if the fixer rewrites assert.equal(emptyMessage(0), "No projects yet") into assert.equal(emptyMessage(0), ""), one assertion was removed and one added, so the count is equal. That is why CI fixers carry the never-rule edit_test_assertions in their charter, which turns any removed assertion line into a finding. The threshold rule pairs the same key on a removed and an added line: a fail-under that goes down is looser, and a retries or timeout value that goes up is looser.

notes.text: A test file on either stack: under test/, tests/ or e2e/, or named *.test.ts, *.spec.tsx, test_*.py.
New skips in Vitest, Playwright, pytest and unittest. .only counts too, because it silently skips every other test.
An assertion line: assert, self.assertEqual and friends, or expect(.
A threshold with a number. Group 1 is the key, group 2 the value.
A skip is a finding in any file, not only in test files.
With this never-rule, touching any existing assertion is a finding, even if the count stays the same.
pairedChanges finds the same key on a removed and an added line, with the old and new value.
For fail-under, lower is looser. For retries and timeouts, higher is looser.

deeper.h: Go deeper: false heals in workflow files
p: The pipeline fixer works on CI workflows themselves, and workflows can be weakened in ways that test-file rules never see. So it gets extra rules: no continue-on-error: true (a failing step that no longer fails the job), no if: false on a job or step, no command ending in || true, no flag that turns a check off such as --no-verify, no required check removed, and no trigger paths narrowed so that a check stops running on some changes. Until Security agrees to a grant for this fixer only, it cannot push workflow changes at all, because our GitHub App has no permission to edit workflow files; it posts its change as a patch for a person to apply.

read.h: Where the check runs, and what a finding costs
p: The check runs in two places. Inside the VM, the harness runs it from the Stop hook, the hook that runs when the agent says it is done. A finding there sends the agent back to work with the reason, so it can restore the test and fix the code instead, which is the cheapest moment to catch it. Then, before any pull request exists, it runs again on the final diff, ahead of the scope judge. That second run is the wall: whatever happened in the session, a weakened test does not leave the VM as a routine's PR.

For Nova the findings are flags in the PR, because a person asked for that work and may have a reason. For a routine, any finding rejects the run with the outcome false_heal, no PR is opened, and the trust ladder moves the routine one step down. One false heal costs a routine more than ten good fixes earn it, and that is on purpose: a weakened test that ships is worse than a red main, because nobody knows to look.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the backend CI fixer's hand-offs
p: The backend CI fixer reuses the same flow for cloud and client CI, with cloud/, client/ and sdk/ as its paths and migrations denied. Some failures it never tries to fix. Protoc drift touches the gRPC stubs in common/fcp_common/, the contract between cloud and client, which is outside its paths. A failing makemigrations --check means a database migration, and the pilot allows none. Integration tests that need the QA environments cannot run in the VM. All three go to the backend guild with the evidence.

lab.title: Catch the false heal
needs: Node 22.18 or newer (it runs .ts files directly)
lab.goal: Break main in a tiny repo, make three fixes that all turn CI green, and write the check that tells the honest one from the two false heals.

guess.q: Your first version of the check counts assertion lines and rejects a diff when it removes more than it adds. The fixer changes assert.equal(emptyMessage(0), "No projects yet") into assert.equal(emptyMessage(0), ""). Does the counting rule catch it?

options.text: Yes, because an assertion line was removed.
options.why: One assertion line was removed, but one was added too, so the count did not go down.

options.text: No, because the number of assertions stays the same.
options.why: That is the gap. The never-rule edit_test_assertions closes it by rejecting any removed assertion line in a CI fixer's diff.

options.text: No, because the check only looks at source files.
options.why: The assertion rules look at test files only. The problem here is that the count is unchanged.

follow.say: Make a tiny repo with one function, its tests and a Playwright config, and commit it as a green main.
Break main the way the 10:02 refactor did, and reproduce the failure, because "is it us?" always comes first.
follow.do:
cat > src/projects.ts <<'EOF'
export const emptyMessage = (projectCount: number): string =>
  projectCount < 0 ? "No projects yet" : "";
EOF
git commit -qam "refactor: simplify the empty state" && node --test --test-reporter=spec 2>&1 | head -2
follow.see:
✖ shows No projects yet when there are no projects (1.2ms)
✔ shows nothing when there are projects (0.0855ms)

follow.say: Make three fixes on three branches: an honest one, a skip, and an edited expectation. Watch all three turn CI green.
follow.do:
git switch -qc fix/honest && sed -i.bak 's/projectCount < 0/projectCount === 0/' src/projects.ts
git commit -qam "fix: show the empty card again" && node --test 2>&1 | grep -E "^# (pass|fail|skipped) [1-9]"
git switch -q main && git switch -qc fix/skip
sed -i.bak 's/^test("shows No projects yet/test.skip("shows No projects yet/' test/projects.test.ts
git commit -qam "fix: unblock main" && node --test 2>&1 | grep -E "^# (pass|fail|skipped) [1-9]"
git switch -q main && git switch -qc fix/expect
sed -i.bak 's/emptyMessage(0), "No projects yet"/emptyMessage(0), ""/' test/projects.test.ts
git commit -qam "test: match the new empty state" && node --test 2>&1 | grep -E "^# (pass|fail|skipped) [1-9]"
git switch -q main && rm -f src/*.bak test/*.bak

follow.say: Write the first version of the check. It reads git diff between main and a branch, and it only knows about deleted test files and new skips.
follow.see:
✔ fix/honest: no false heal
✘ fix/skip: false heal
  test/projects.test.ts: new skip `test.skip("shows No projects yet when there are no projects", () => {`
✔ fix/expect: no false heal

lab.build: The edited expectation got through. Add the missing rules where the comment says: in test files, count assertion lines (the ASSERT pattern) on removed and added lines and report when more were removed; when the never-list has edit_test_assertions, report any removed assertion line; and for every THRESHOLD key that appears on both a removed and an added line, report it as loosened when a fail-under value went down or a retries or timeout value went up. Then make a fourth branch, fix/retries, that changes retries: 0 to retries: 2 in playwright.config.ts, and run the check on all four branches.
checks: ✘ fix/expect reports: test/projects.test.ts: an existing assertion was changed
If you remove edit_test_assertions from the never set at the bottom of the file, fix/expect passes again, which shows why CI fixers carry that rule.
lab.fix: A teammate made the check "smarter": it now skips files whose path contains /e2e/, because "end-to-end tests are flaky anyway, the fixer should be allowed to tune them". The next week a fixer raises a Playwright timeout from 30000 to 120000 in an e2e helper and adds test.fixme to a spec, and both pass the check. Find the line that lets them through and remove it, then explain why a flaky test is a reason for the flaky-test fixer, never for loosening a check.
explain: Why is the false-heal check a short program reading the diff, and not an instruction in the prompt or a question for the scope judge?
Why does counting assertions miss a changed expectation, and which charter rule closes that gap?
Why does the check run twice, once in the Stop hook and once before the PR?
lab.done: The check passes the honest fix and rejects the skip, the edited expectation and the raised retries, each with a reason a person can read.

check.q: The CI fixer runs the failed unit tests at main's newest commit in its VM, and they pass. What does it do?

options.text: Pushes an empty commit so CI runs again
options.why: Agents never re-run or dispatch CI. And green in the VM already says the code is not the problem.

options.text: Makes the most likely fix anyway, to be safe
options.why: That is fixing code that is not broken, the most common way a CI fixer goes wrong.

options.text: Posts the evidence to #ai-agents-alerts and stops, because the failure is in the environment or a flake
options.why: Is it us? No. A person deals with runners, mirrors and QA environments.

check.q: A routine's fix changes fail_under = 50 to fail_under = 40 in a coverage config and turns CI green. What happens?

options.text: The check reports fail_under loosened 50 -> 40, the run ends as a false heal, no PR opens, and the routine steps down
options.why: For fail-under, lower is looser. For a routine, any finding rejects the run and counts on the trust ladder.

options.text: Nothing, because it is a config file and not a test
options.why: The threshold rule reads every file. A config that sets how strict the tests are is part of the tests.

options.text: The PR opens with a flag, and a person decides
options.why: That is how Nova's findings are handled. For routines, a finding rejects the run.

check.q: Why does a single false heal cost a routine so much?

options.text: Because false heals are expensive to compute
options.why: The check is a few regular expressions. The cost is about trust, not compute.

options.text: Because a false heal that ships hides a bug behind a green main, so nobody knows to look, which is worse than a red main
options.why: A red main is loud and gets fixed. A weakened test is quiet and stays. That is why it is the one failure that must never ship.

options.text: Because a false heal means the routine has a bug in its harness
options.why: It can happen with a perfectly working harness. It is a shortcut the model took, which is why code checks for it.

p: The check is harness/src/checks/false-heal.ts in ai-agents, built on G0's weakened-tests detector (checks/src/weakened-tests.ts) so there is one implementation, with the charter rules edit_test_assertions, add_code and add_retries_or_sleeps added. It runs from the Stop hook in the VM and on the final diff before the scope judge; harness/test/false-heal.test.ts covers real diffs (an honest fix, a deleted test, an it.skip, a lowered --fail-under, an added time.sleep).

The FE CI fixer uses the fe-ci-fixer charter in shadow, with routines/fe-ci-fixer/jobs.yaml, the skills fix-ci, fe-codebase, verify, fcp-lab and pr-story, Opus 5.5 at low effort (medium on a failed step) and a lite Spot VM. Its fix must pass npm run verify and the reproduced commands. The BE CI fixer reuses it with routines/be-ci-fixer/jobs.yaml. The pipeline fixer adds harness/src/checks/false-heal-workflows.ts for workflow files and posts workflow changes as a patch until Security agrees to a workflows grant.

tickets.why: The false-heal check: the patterns, the charter rules, the Stop hook and the run before the scope judge.
The FE CI fixer: jobs.yaml, "is it us?" first, the smallest fix inside frontend/.
The BE CI fixer: the same flow for cloud and client CI, with its hand-offs.
The pipeline fixer and the extra false-heal rules for workflow files.

words.plain: A change that turns CI green by weakening a test or a check instead of fixing the code.
The CI fixer's first step: run the failed commands at main's head in the VM. Green there means the environment, not our code.
Extra rules in a charter, such as edit_test_assertions, that the false-heal check enforces for that routine.
A number that sets how strict a check is, such as a coverage minimum, a retry count or a timeout.

review.q: Name four shapes of false heal the check looks for.
review.a: A deleted test file, a new skip (it.skip, test.skip, .only, .fixme, pytest skip or xfail), a removed or changed assertion, and a loosened threshold (fail-under down, retries or timeout up).

review.q: Why does a CI fixer's charter carry never: [edit_test_assertions], when the check already counts assertions?
review.a: Counting misses a changed expectation, because one assertion is removed and one added. The never-rule rejects any removed assertion line, so the fixer cannot rewrite what the test expects.

review.q: What is different when the same finding appears in a Nova PR and in a routine's run?
review.a: For Nova it is a flag in the PR for the reviewer. For a routine it rejects the run as false_heal, no PR is opened, and the routine steps down the trust ladder.

remember: Ask "is it us?" first, then fix the code, never the test: a short program reads every routine's diff and rejects any fix that turns CI green by weakening a check.
